body:
Monitoring an individual and monitoring a population

Health monitoring may occur at 2 different levels. Individual monitoring follows measurements or clinical findings in a particular person, such as blood pressure, blood glucose or treatment progress. Public-health surveillance involves the systematic collection, analysis and use of information about health events in a population.

Surveillance helps health authorities recognise unusual disease patterns and respond before an outbreak becomes larger. For example, an unexpected rise in cases of acute diarrhoeal illness in one area may require investigation of possible common exposures, including water and food sources.

A surveillance alert is not necessarily proof of an outbreak. Reports must be assessed, and investigation may reveal several possible causes. The purpose is to detect important signals early enough for appropriate public-health action.

Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme

India's Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), under the National Centre for Disease Control, supports reporting and monitoring of epidemic-prone diseases. The Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) supports digital reporting, analysis and monitoring of disease trends.

IDSP uses 3 important categories of routine reporting:

FormType of informationUsual reporting personnel
SSyndromic or suspected cases based on a pattern of symptomsHealth workers
PPresumptive cases based on clinical assessmentClinicians or medical officers
LLaboratory-confirmed casesLaboratory personnel

The distinction reflects the level of evidence. Symptoms alone may suggest several possible diseases. Clinical assessment narrows the possibilities, while an appropriate laboratory test can provide evidence of a specific infection.

District, state and national surveillance units examine reported trends. When an unusual increase or cluster requires investigation, Rapid Response Teams may assess the situation and support control measures.

Digital health records are different from surveillance

The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) seeks to enable digital exchange of health information within India's healthcare system. An Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) number is a unique 14-digit health identifier used to help link and access digital health records, with consent-based sharing.

A digital health record can include information such as prescriptions, laboratory reports and other medical documents. It supports continuity of care when a person consults different healthcare providers.

ABHA is a digital health identity, not a diagnostic test or an automatic health-insurance entitlement. It helps with identifying, linking and sharing health records; it does not itself establish the presence of a disease or provide treatment.

Telemedicine: eSanjeevani

eSanjeevani is India's national telemedicine service. It enables consultations using communication technology, including patient-to-doctor and facility-supported doctor-to-doctor models. Telemedicine can improve access to professional advice when patients and clinicians are in different locations.

It differs from ABHA because its central purpose is remote healthcare consultation, rather than creating a health identifier or linking records.

A Ministry of Health and Family Welfare release dated 6 October 2026 reported that eSanjeevani had crossed 50 crore cumulative teleconsultations on 15 September 2026, across all 36 states and Union Territories. This is a reported milestone for that date, not a live total for 3 November 2026.

Gujarat's mother-and-child and community-health systems

e-Mamta

The Government of Gujarat introduced e-Mamta as a name-based mother-and-child tracking information system. Its documented scope includes registering and following pregnant women, children aged 0–6 years and adolescents for services such as antenatal care, postnatal care, immunisation and nutrition. Its purpose is to help identify beneficiaries who need scheduled services and those who may have missed them.

TeCHO+

Gujarat's TeCHO+, described in National Health Mission documentation as Technology Enabled Community Health Operations, is a mobile and web-based system designed to assist community health workers and health administrators. Documented functions include beneficiary tracking, service reminders, referral support and monitoring of primary healthcare delivery.

These systems illustrate an important distinction: individual service tracking helps workers follow up with particular people, while disease surveillance examines population-level trends that may require broader investigation.

Comparing the main systems

System or programmePrincipal purposeKey distinction
IDSP and IHIPSurveillance of disease trends and outbreaksPopulation-level reporting and response
ABDM and ABHADigital health identity and health-record exchangeABHA is a 14-digit identifier
eSanjeevaniRemote medical consultationTelemedicine rather than surveillance
e-MamtaTracking maternal, child and adolescent health servicesName-based beneficiary follow-up
TeCHO+Digital support for community healthcare deliveryHealth-worker and service-management functions

These descriptions follow government programme documents and public information available by the 3 November 2026 content cutoff. The documented purpose of a system should not be mistaken for verified live usage, complete geographic coverage or unchanged operating arrangements at every health facility.

Connecting organisms, ecosystems and public-health tools

The main biological ideas form a continuous explanation. Organisms depend on nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion. Their characteristics and adaptations influence survival in particular environments. Organisms interact through food chains, nutrient cycling and other ecological relationships. Human disease risks may arise when pathogens, vectors, people and environmental conditions interact.

Public-health tools act on different parts of this chain. Diagnostics help identify conditions in individuals. Health measurements help monitor body functions. Water and sanitation measures reduce exposure to pathogens. Surveillance systems identify patterns across populations. Digital records and telemedicine support access to, and continuity of, healthcare.

Prelims focus

  • IDSP monitors disease trends; IHIP supports digital surveillance reporting.
  • IDSP reporting distinguishes S: syndromic, P: presumptive and L: laboratory-confirmed cases.
  • ABHA is a 14-digit digital health identifier under ABDM.
  • eSanjeevani provides telemedicine consultations.
  • Gujarat's e-Mamta concerns name-based tracking of mother-and-child services; TeCHO+ supports community healthcare delivery.
  • Trap: Disease surveillance, telemedicine, digital health identification and beneficiary tracking serve different purposes.

pictures.caption: Surveillance reporting supports detection, investigation and response to unusual disease trends.

title: Public-Health Surveillance and Digital Health Systems in India and Gujarat
